assessment: The incumbent remains credible for simpler repeated work: both workers completed repeated three-compartment orders in seven to nine minutes (D2-O6), close to the target. However, the overall median was 11 minutes, five customers reported component problems, and only seven of ten observed users succeeded unaided (D2-O2–O4). Mixed batches contained every extreme delay, but layout complexity and switching are confounded. Overlapping partition widths among first- and second-attempt insertions (D2-O5) limit a width-only explanation; slot dimensions and orientation remain unmeasured. Preassembly's possible checking benefit is a hypothesis, not demonstrated protection against omissions.

openings.claim: Layout switching may add selection and checking work that an order-specific parts staging step could reduce while retaining full assembly.
openings.delta: Test whether the incumbent can meet the time target through order preparation before changing its assembly policy.
openings.prediction: For the same target layout and color, orders following a different layout take longer in selection/checking; staging reduces that difference without increasing component errors.
openings.probe: Use existing parts and slips for matched repeated-layout and switched-layout trials, with and without bench staging. Counterbalance workers and order. Record selection, staging, insertion, checking and packing separately; include staging in total time and audit contents against each order.
assumptions: Trials fit spare capacity before the fixed delivery date; otherwise defer them.
Staging uses existing materials and preserves dimensions, assortment, removable partitions, counts and colors.

openings.claim: Does short-partition confusion persist when contents and insertion fit are verified and customers receive only their ordered-layout diagram?
openings.delta: Separate instruction ambiguity from incorrect contents or physical insertion difficulty; the reported partition problems do not identify a single cause.
openings.prediction: If diagram ambiguity contributes, verified kits with an order-specific diagram produce fewer short-partition placement questions than verified kits with the current three-layout diagram.
openings.probe: Randomize ten willing participants between diagrams using matched, verified kits. Record unaided ordered-layout completion, misplaced short partitions, questions and insertion retries. Treat results as directional; this sample cannot establish the pilot success rate.
assumptions: Existing board samples and diagrams suffice without delaying delivery.
Any adopted diagram change must keep initial and recurring costs within the stipulated caps; product specifications remain intact.
